title: How NOT to spot a fake natty: size/strength discrepancy
summary: NH rejects the idea that being big but weak proves steroid use: leverages, limb length, muscle insertions and training style all affect strength. Using a thought experiment comparing weekly 1RM front squats with 5-rep sets, he argues that accumulated volume, not max strength, drives hypertrophy, and that 'strength' means something different in bodybuilding than in powerlifting.

claims.claim: Being big but weak on the main lifts is not proof of steroid use; that reasoning ignores leverages, limb length, muscle insertions and how the person trained.
NH agrees only partly with the popular idea that there's no hypertrophy rep range and that getting strong gets you big: training only for strength in one rep range builds size, but less of it.

Thought experiment: over 30 weekly sessions, a strength trainee does one rep of 275 lb on front squat each time while a hypertrophy trainee does 225 lb for 5 reps each time; the second moves far more total weight despite the weaker max.
Volume, many reps over a long period, is what grows muscle, so the higher-volume trainee grows more.
Strength isn't only moving something once; it can be moving it five times, several times in a workout, or several times a week, and it means different things in bodybuilding and powerlifting.
Natural lifters should drop size-strength discrepancy as a fake-natty indicator.
